articles.title: Veteran journalist Philip Lustre posts bail on cyberlibel raps
articles.summary: Lustre, 72, has posted bail amounting to P48,000 and was released on Saturday, October 24.

blocks.text: October 25, 2026 | 11:07am

Veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. is escorted by police officers at the Quezon City Police District (QCPD) Kamuning Station 10 in Quezon City to undergo physical and medical examination following his arrest on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026.
The STAR / Miguel de Guzman
MANILA, Philippines — Veteran Journalist Philip Lustre has secured provisional liberty after posting bail on cyberlibel charges filed against him.
Lustre, 72, has posted bail amounting to P48,000 and was released on Saturday, October 24.
He was arrested on Saturday while attending a news forum based on a warrant of arrest issued by the Regional Trial Court, Branch 10, in Davao City.
According to Lustre’s lawyer, Dino de Leon, the veteran journalist was unaware of the complaint before his arrest.

“Per Mr. Lustre, he is unaware of any pending criminal charge or preliminary investigation against him prior to this arrest. As of writing, we still do not know the specific particulars of the case nor the identity of the complainant as the arrest happened on a weekend when the court that supposedly issued the warrant is closed,” De Leon said in a statement.

“In any event, we are looking at what appears to be a deprivation of Mr. Lustre’s right to due process at the preliminary investigation stage where no subpoena or notice was ever served on or received by him. In other words, he was not even given the chance to ventilate his defenses or air his side prior to the issuance of the warrant of arrest,” he added.

De Leon also pointed out that the arrest warrant listed an incorrect address: the Media Resource Plaza Building along Mola and Pasong Tirad Streets in Makati City, rather than Lustre's actual residence.
Lustre is the author of the book “Kill, kill, kill,” which tackled extrajudicial killings in the country.

In a separate statement, the Presidential Task Force on Media Security (PTFOMS) expressed concern over Lustre's October 24 arrest, urging authorities to respect his constitutional rights and grant him immediate access to legal counsel and medical care.

“PTFOMS takes serious note of concerns raised by media organizations that libel and cyberlibel laws have been weaponized to target critical voices, intimidate journalists, and discourage reporting on matters of public interest. These concerns call for careful review and effective safeguards against the abuse of legal processes,” the PTFOMS said.

articles.title: [Two Pronged] My love and sex life are complicated, and I want a committed relationship
articles.summary: Our letter sender is wondering about desire, life direction, and relationships as she finds someone she's compatible with sexually, but who can't stay in the Philippines and may not be able to commit…

blocks.text: Rappler’s People section runs an advice column by couple Jeremy Baer and clinical psychologist Dr. Margarita Holmes.

Jeremy has a master’s degree in law from Oxford University. A banker of 37 years who worked in three continents, he has been training with Dr. Holmes for the last 10 years as co-lecturer and, occasionally, as co-therapist, especially with clients whose financial concerns intrude into their daily lives.
Together, they have written two books: Love Triangles: Understanding the Macho-Mistress Mentality and Imported Love: Filipino-Foreign Liaisons.

Dear Dr. Holmes and Mr. Baer, I wonder these days why people enter relationships. While getting in one is not the center of my life, I have questions about the intersection between desire, life direction, and relationships.

I’m now at a point where I’ve experienced the most satisfying sex I could ever imagine with someone but he will not live in the Philippines permanently and when he leaves he knows he cannot maintain an LDR (long distance relationship).
I found myself in another two month relationship with a man with a volatile libido. I ended up walking on eggshells, crashing my libido badly.
I reconnected with the first guy. I was able to let my guard down and bare my raw self and act in a way that I’ve never been before.
Right now, this man is someone I can’t let go of but still I can’t just plan my life around him, so it’s a dilemma, a floating connection.
I now allow myself to talk to anyone that makes me happy. I don’t become loyal anymore to anything hypothetical and I have more reservations now.
I’m also deeply aware and learned the hard way that I don’t want to feel ever again that I’m good enough to f*** but not worthy enough to commit to.
– Anna
Dear Anna,
Relationships are complex and come in many forms, as it is clear you already know.

You ask why people enter them yet in reality you have answered your own question already. A relationship offers the opportunity to reveal yourself fully and safely with someone else without having to sacrifice your own dignity and integrity, an aim that is achievable but often only partially.
The two relationships you describe illustrate this. The “eggshell” one showed you what happens whenthere is no safety — having to deal with mood shifts can kill desire.

The “reconnection” one demonstrates the effect of safety – you can reveal your true self. The contrast is critical and can usefully inform your future. However, the way you describe your current attachment is scarcely ideal. He is someone you cannot let go of but cannot plan a future with either, or as you label it, this is a floating relationship.
That the sex is extraordinary is a bonus but also a distraction.
After all, great sex doesn’t mean that he is the right partner for you any more than a missing label means that he isn’t.
The real issue is: is he willing to move forward and label your relationship or are you shoring it up with hope that may be misplaced?

A way forward would be to ask him: what does he want from the relationship? Is he willing to build something? His answer, or avoidance, will tell you much more than any guesswork on your part and if in the final analysis he wants intimacy without commitment, at least you will know where you stand.
Best wishes,
– JAF Baer
Dear Anna:
Thank you very much for your letter. You ask a very important question: Why do people get into relationships?
A cursory search will give you a plethora of reasons, but in truth one can probably divide said reasons into two:

items: neuroscientific ones — mirror neurons, oxytocin, etc. but one of the simplest ways to describe this is that we are social beings that need relationships because our brains are wired to connect with others; and
practical and social reasons, such as when relationships result in children, it is much easier to raise the kids when said relationships continue; to avoid loneliness, etc.

blocks.text: From the theoretical standpoint above, let us now proceed to a more personal level and try to gain a larger perspective on your love and sex life.

At the moment, you seem to not just want, but actually need relationships with the opposite sex. In the last four months, you have been in a relationship first, with man A, whom you felt safe enough to have terrific sex with; but when his lack of commitment hurt you so much, you went to volatile man B who, thankfully, you realized after 2 months was not the sort of man you wanted in your life.

The following (4th) month, you went back to man A, not just because the sex was, once more, absolutely fantastic, but because you reveled in being the woman you felt you truly were (and you could well be right) when with him. And because you felt complete, cherished and truly seen by him, you wanted the relationship to continue.

Yet even as the relationship continued, man A was honest enough to say it couldn’t last forever because for whatever reason, he could not or would not stay in the Philippines forever. Man A, despite knowing that you could end the relationship prematurely (in his eyes-because I have a feeling not just the sex, but the while experience of being with you was also mind boggling for him), was honest enough to continue telling you the truth.
Some writers divide people into two types:
“Those who run away from something” or “Those who run towards something.”

Actually, I would include a third type of person: those who run towards something (like a seemingly perfect relationship with man A) but then realize it is best for their mental health to run away from that same something.
I would like to say that your last two paragraphs show what a mature person you have become. And this is true but, perhaps, not the complete truth.

If you can hold off from sex with someone you genuinely like whom you know also genuinely likes you, is willing to commit to you but is honest enough to say, but I am not sure if this commitment will be forever, then terrific.
You can still have a warm, funny, fulfilling relationship with him but not have sex.
Another option is to believe that just because a relationship (with sex) doesn’t last forever, it does not mean it is empty or worthless.
If you can truly manage one of these two options, then I say, “you go, girl!” But I am not sure you can.
This is not to demean you in any way. This is merely a recognition that people are different and some feel they need sex more than others.
If one is particularly blessed with the right experiences and/or the right therapy, one’s needs and one’s wants can live together harmoniously OR this can be a goal worth aspiring to.

And if one is self compassionate enough to forgive oneself for the same “mistakes” with the same generosity one could forgive one’s best friend, then each relationship you have can be a learning experience.
Hopefully, each relationship can also have more positive than negative elements in them.
That way, in time, you might agree with what the brilliant psychoanalyst and humanistic philosopher Erich Fromm once wrote in his 1956 book The Art of Loving:
Immature love: I love you because I need you.Mature love: I need you because I love you.
The best of luck to you – to US! — my fellow work in progress
– MG Holmes
Life got complicated? Write to our Two Pronged duo at twopronged@rappler.com.

articles.title: TRB all set to assist motorists during Undas 2026
articles.summary: The Toll Regulatory Board on Sunday said measures are in place to assist motorists as the country will observe All Saints' Day (Undas) and All Souls' Day on November 1 to 2, respectively.

blocks.text: Published October 25, 2026 10:58am
The Toll Regulatory Board (TRB) on Sunday said measures are in place to assist motorists as the country will observe All Saints' Day (Undas) and All Souls' Day on November 1 to 2, respectively.
TRB spokesperson Julius Corpus said "Oplan Biyaheng Ayos" will be implemented from October 29 to November 30 to ensure a smooth traffic flow along expressways.

He said all toll gates will remain open to avoid traffic congestion, while lane assistance personnel will be deployed to help motorists experiencing issues with their radio frequency identification (RFID) tags.

“We will also deploy additional patrol vehicles, toll trucks, fire trucks, ambulances, emergency medical service, and incident response teams to help motorists,” Corpus told Super Radyo dzBB in an interview.
He added that dedicated personnel will be deployed to manage the traffic inside service stations or stopovers and ensure clean and adequate facilities.
Free towing service will also be available, excluding repair service.
On Saturday, the Land Transportation Office (LTO) said there was still a normal flow of people at two major bus terminals in Metro Manila one week before the commemoration of Undas.
The LTO is implementing “Oplan Biyaheng Ayos” for Undas, inspecting Cubao, Quezon CIty and the Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange (PITX).
PITX is expecting around 1.9 million passengers this year amid the exodus for this year's All Saints' Day (Undas) break.
Many Filipinos are expected to go to their hometowns for the Undas break to pay their respects to their departed loved ones.
All Saints' Day will fall on Sunday, November 1, while All Souls' Day will be on Monday, November 2. Both are special non-working days. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Obama attacks Trump as he campaigns for Democrats ahead of midterm elections
articles.summary: Obama said the election was "the last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration".

blocks.text: Former President Barack Obama has attacked the Trump administration over the Iran war and high consumer prices as he hit the campaign trail for Democrats ahead of the US midterm elections.
"This election is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration," Obama told crowds in Ohio on Saturday.
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump touted his administration's immigration and tariff policies at a rally in Georgia, telling supporters "we're in the golden age of America".
The midterm elections on 3 November will decide which party controls Congress for the rest of Trump's term, and therefore how easy it is for the president to carry out his plans.
Early voting has already begun and Trump cast his ballot on Saturday in Florida alongside his wife First Lady Melania Trump.
Speaking on Saturday in Ohio and Michigan, Obama targeted Trump and his cabinet members, at one point mocking the president's attempt to redecorate the White House.

"After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, 'enough is enough,'" the former president said in Cleveland.

Obama said he sympathised with voters who rejected Democrats in 2024 over economic and inflation concerns following the Covid pandemic. But he said Trump had only himself to blame for the current state of the economy.
"If you thought everything was too expensive before 'you know who'," he said, referring to Trump without using his name, "everything is more expensive now".
Trump, meanwhile, acknowledged that oil prices were "temporarily high" but said "our country is getting stronger and stronger all the time, and those pump prices are going to come down".
The Republican president has faced significant pressure to lower fuel prices, which have jumped due to the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

Talking up the economy, Trump told the crowd in Perry "we're taking in massive amounts of money through tariffs", and repeated his pledge to offer every adult American a $5,000 (£3,700) payout if Republicans win both chambers of Congress.
He also took aim at the Democrats, telling the crowd they would "loot your wealth" and "annihilate your borders".
Using derogatory language, he accused the Democrats of trying to open up immigration from Libya, Yemen, Haiti and Somalia - countries which he described as "terror-infested".

Describing a previous meeting with several senators, he recalled: "I said, 'Why do we always have to take people from shithouse countries? Why can't we take people from, like, well... Norway, Sweden? Why not Denmark?'"

articles.title: New York Archdiocese to pay $800 million to sex abuse survivors
articles.summary: Around 1,300 survivors agreed to the $800 million payout from the Catholic Church, marking one of the largest clergy abuse settlements in the US.

image.caption: Each of the survivors will receive at least $250,000, according to media reportsImage: Yuki Iwamura/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Survivors of sexual abuse by Catholic clergy accepted an $800 million (€714 million) settlement with the Archdiocese of New York, ending years of lawsuits, their lawyers announced on Saturday.

"The unanimous agreement of survivors who filed claims against the Archdiocese of New York marks a powerful moment in the pursuit of justice," Jeff Anderson, an attorney representing survivors, said in a statement.
"Through their courage, sacrifice, and determination, survivors have helped bring about a reckoning and a meaningful step toward accountability," it added.
The agreement was proposed by the Archdiocese of New York in May and is set to be formally signed in early November.
Each plaintiff to receive at least $250,000

Around 1,300 survivors are included in the agreement. Each of them is expected to receive at least $250,000, according to The New York Times, which broke the story. Some larger payouts are possible depending on the extent of the abuse.

"We are on the verge of being able to, please God, bring some measure of healing and reconciliation to all victim-survivors," New York Archbishop Ronald Hicks wrote in an email to clergy confirming the settlement.

"This agreement will also allow the archdiocese to turn its full attention once again to its mission of preaching the Gospel, healing the sick, caring for the poor and needy, welcoming the stranger, and educating our children," he added.

Hicks was appointed by the US-born Pope Leo in December 2025, replacing conservative Cardinal Timothy Dolan. Before leaving the post, Dolan had started a process of creating a $300 million fund to compensate victims of sexual abuse.
The deal announced on Saturday is one ​of the largest payouts over clergy sex abuse in ​the ‌US — second ‌only ​to an $880 million settlement reached by the Archdiocese of Los Angeles in 2024.
Catholic Church faces flurry of US abuse cases

articles.title: Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi ‘sounds strong’ but is isolated, son says
articles.summary: Kim Aris tells the Guardian chance to speak with detained Nobel laureate was ‘public relations’ move from military leaders Myanmar’s former democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi appears to be in good…

blocks.text: Myanmar’s former democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi appears to be in good physical and mental health but is living in near-complete isolation, her son has said after the first call with his 81-year-old mother in more than five years.

“She still sounds certainly all there mentally, and physically she sounds strong,” Kim Aris said. “I don’t think she has anybody outside of the military or the police around her, so essentially she’s been held in solitary confinement from what I gather.”

After being deposed in a 2021 military coup, the Nobel Peace prize laureate has been moved to an unspecified location in the capital. “I’m still not entirely sure where she is,” said Aris. “I think it’s a residence in Naypyidaw, which is fenced off and it has a scrubby bit of land around it.”

blocks.caption: Aung San Suu Kyi talks on the phone with her son on Thursday, in a photo released by the Myanmar presidential office. Photograph: Myanmar President Spokesperson Office/AP

blocks.text: Aris, who has lived in the UK most of his life and whose late father was a British historian, was allowed to speak to his mother on Thursday at the Myanmar embassy in London. While he welcomed the chance to talk, he said the invitation was part of a “public relations” campaign by the country’s military leaders.

The former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing has sought to rebuild international diplomatic ties, and in April switched his military fatigues for civilian clothes after elections that were widely condemned as a sham.

Activists have long demanded “proof of life” for Aung San Suu Kyi, as well as scores of other political prisoners. In August, she was finally photographed during a Red Cross visit. Last week, a government spokesperson published images of her smiling in a wood-panelled room as officials delivered two gardening books given to her as gifts by Britain’s King Charles. A paper calendar on the wall behind her showed the date.

Aris said these photo-ops were well-known stunts that the regime had used before to pretend his mother, a national icon, was being treated fairly. The daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San has spent much of her life since the late 1980s in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements.

“She remains completely shut off from the rest of the world. I think she’s unaware of what’s happening outside of where she is because she’s not allowed any newspapers or radio or television,” Aris said. “She’s been locked up for five years on trumped-up, politically motivated charges and she should be free.”

Ruled for decades by generals and suffering from western sanctions, Myanmar experienced a brief democratic moment after Aung San Suu Kyi was allowed to run in a 2015 election that her party overwhelmingly won. She took up the role of “state counsellor” under a civilian-military power-sharing agreement.

blocks.caption: Aung San Suu Kyi shakes hands with Myanmar’s military commander-in-chief Min Aung Hlaing (left) in December 2015. Photograph: Lynn Bo Bo/EPA

blocks.text: Her international reputation was soon tarnished after the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims. Aung San Suu Kyi flew to the international court of justice in The Hague, where she said she acknowledged military units might have used “disproportionate force”, but defended the government against accusations of genocide.

Aris said that his mother was never “silent” on the Rohingya crisis and what she said on the issue “could fill volumes”. Under her leadership, Myanmar launched a domestic inquiry and appointed the former UN chief Kofi Annan to head a commission.
He added that as state counsellor, Aung San Suu Kyi was “always walking on a tightrope”, knowing the military could strip her of her fragile power at any moment.

“The very hard-won nascent democracy that she was trying to lead was holding on to things by a thread,” he said. “The military could have taken over at any point, and they were doing their best to make my mother’s situation a lot more difficult and to undermine her position. And I think in that respect they did a pretty good job.”
The 2021 power grab by the military triggered a civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to conflict monitors.

Aris said the level of public global support for his mother had “dwindled incredibly” since the Rohingya crisis and that the whole country was now suffering from a lack of international attention. While many governments have called for Aung San Suu Kyi’s release, she is not treated as the beloved international figure that she once was.

“Never mind my mother, the fact that people ignore what’s happening in Burma shouldn’t be down to what was being done to the Rohingya,” he said, using the country’s former name. “And that seems to be the case sometimes, that people say: ‘Oh, well, look how the Rohingya were treated. We can ignore what’s happening in Burma.’”

articles.title: ITCZ to bring rain to Palawan, Visayas, Mindanao on October 25 — PAGASA
articles.summary: The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) may bring rain to parts of the Visayas, Mindanao and Southern Luzon, the state weather bureau PAGASA said on Sunday, October 25.

blocks.text: October 25, 2026 | 9:12am
Pedestrians and motorists brave heavy rain along United Nations Avenue in Manila.
The Star / Ryan Baldemor
MANILA, Philippines — The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) may bring rain to parts of the Visayas, Mindanao and Southern Luzon, the state weather bureau PAGASA said on Sunday, October 25.
In its daily weather forecast issued 4 a.m., PAGASA said the ITCZ may bring cloudy skies with scattered rain showers and thunderstorms to the Visayas, Mindanao, the Bicol Region, Romblon and Palawan.
The state weather bureau warned residents in these areas of possible flash floods or landslides due to moderate to, at times, heavy rains.
Meanwhile, Metro Manila and the rest of the country may experience partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rain showers or thunderstorms caused by localized thunderstorms.
PAGASA also warned residents in these areas of possible flash floods or landslides during severe thunderstorms.

articles.title: PH, Holy See mark 75 years of diplomatic ties, reaffirm commitment to peace, justice
articles.summary: The Philippines and the Holy See marked the 75th anniversary of their diplomatic relations on Friday with a Eucharistic celebration at the Santuario di San Giovanni Battista De La Salle in Rome,…

blocks.text: ROME — The Philippines and the Holy See marked the 75th anniversary of their diplomatic relations on Friday with a Eucharistic celebration at the Santuario di San Giovanni Battista De La Salle in Rome, reaffirming their shared commitment to peace, justice, and human dignity.

The Mass was presided over by Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin who highlighted the historical significance of the relationship and called for stronger dialogue and cooperation in addressing the challenges facing the world today.

The milestone also coincided with the 65th anniversary of the Pontificio Collegio Filippino in Rome, an institution dedicated to supporting the formation and studies of Filipino priests and seminarians.
Cardinal Parolin: Dialogue is essential to peace

In his homily, Cardinal Parolin recalled that diplomatic relations between the Philippines and the Holy See were formally established on April 8, 1951, during the pontificate of Pope Pius XII and the presidency of Elpidio Quirino.
He described the relationship as an indelible part of the shared history of the two sides, strengthened over the decades through mutual respect, religious ties, and diplomatic engagement.

Among the important milestones he highlighted were papal visits to the Philippines, visits by Philippine presidents to the Vatican, and the 2008 agreement concerning the cultural heritage of the Philippine Catholic Church.

Emphasizing the importance of diplomacy in a world marked by tensions and conflicts, Cardinal Parolin said, “In international relations, dialogue is an irreplaceable diplomatic tool for preventing conflicts and rebuilding bonds of trust.”
He urged both sides to continue strengthening their diplomatic ties and renewing their commitment to peace, justice, and the dignity of every human person.
“Whether we work in politics, diplomacy, culture, business, trade, or any other field, we are all called to be architects of peace and active builders of justice in today's world,” he said.
The cardinal also stressed the need to protect human dignity amid rapid technological development, warning that progress can benefit only a privileged few while leaving others behind.
“We must be the guardians of humanity, promoting the human dignity of all,” he emphasized.

Cardinal Pietro Parolin, Vatican secretary of state, recalls that diplomatic relations between the Philippines and the Holy See began on April 8, 1951, during his homily at a Mass held on the 75th anniversary of PH-Holy See diplomatic ties at the Santuario di San Giovanni Battista De La Salle in Rome on October 23, 2026. PIA GONZALEZ-ABUCAY
Church's growing Filipino leadership

In his remarks, Philippine Ambassador to the Holy See Raphael Perpetuo Lotilla reflected on the 75-year diplomatic relationship, highlighting the Holy See's continued support for Filipino participation and leadership in the Catholic Church.

“Significant in the 75 years of relationship has been the sustained support extended by the Holy See to deepen and reinforce Filipino participation and leadership in the Church in the Philippines,” Lotilla said.
He noted that the Catholic Church in the Philippines has developed a strong identity and leadership, with Filipino clergy and religious serving communities both at home and around the world.

Today, the Filipino Catholic community continues to contribute significantly to the life of the universal Church, reflecting the country's longstanding Catholic tradition and its growing international presence.
Pontificio Collegio Filippino celebrates 65 years

Lotilla also highlighted the 65th anniversary of the founding of the Pontificio Collegio Filippino in Rome, which provides Filipino priests and seminarians with opportunities for further studies and formation.

“The second milestone we are celebrating tonight is the 65th anniversary of the founding of the Pontificio Collegio Filippino in Rome, established to facilitate the studies of Filipino priests and seminarians,” he said.
The institution has played an important role in supporting the formation of Filipino clergy and strengthening their contribution to the Catholic Church in the Philippines and beyond.
Commemorative stamp
A highlight of the celebration was the unveiling of a commemorative postage stamp marking the 75th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the Holy See and the Philippines.

The unveiling was led by Cardinal Parolin and Archbishop Emilio Nappa, secretary general of the Governorate of Vatican City State, alongside Philippine Secretary of Foreign Affairs Ma. Theresa P. Lazaro and Lotilla. The officials also signed the commemorative stamp to mark the occasion.

The stamp features St. Peter’s Basilica, an open shell containing a pearl symbolizing the Philippines as the “Pearl of the Orient Seas,” and the flags of both states. These elements reflect the shared Christian faith, enduring friendship, and longstanding cooperation between the two nations.

“This stamp, created by the Philatelic and Numismatic Office of the Vatican City State, celebrates the constant harmony, mutual enrichment, and shared purpose depicting this long friendship. It expresses in a single image our common Christian identity and the bonds of fraternity that unite us. It is a testament of a longstanding and solid tie of friendship and mutual cooperation,” said Archbishop Nappa.
Lazaro underscored the importance of faith in shaping the identity and values of the Filipino people.

“For the more than eighty-five million Filipino Catholics, our faith anchors our identity and values as Filipinos and collective nation. This commemorative stamp serves as a tangible symbol for the 75th anniversary of this establishment of diplomatic relations,” Lazaro said.
She noted that, like other postage stamps, the commemorative issue crosses borders, carries messages, and documents significant moments in history.

As nations navigate an increasingly complex world marked by technological advancements and uncertainties, Lazaro reaffirmed the Philippines’ commitment to peace, stability, and dialogue. She also emphasized the country’s continued cooperation with like-minded partners, including the Holy See, in addressing challenges that require collective action.

The event was attended by members of the diplomatic corps from various embassies, Philippine ambassadors to Southern European countries, priests, religious sisters, and members of the Filipino community.
The celebration concluded with a diplomatic reception, bringing together guests to commemorate the longstanding friendship and cooperation between the Holy See and the Philippines. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: California leaders rebuke Trump administration’s push over alleged noncitizen voting
articles.summary:
Election personnel concerned directive to ‘quickly’ verify 20,000 ballots could disenfranchise citizens

California’s top leaders have rebuked the Trump administration’s efforts to quash…

blocks.text: California’s top leaders have rebuked the Trump administration’s efforts to quash alleged noncitizen voting.
Less than two weeks before the midterms, federal prosecutors called upon California election officials to verify within 48 hours a list of about 20,000 ballots belonging to suspected noncitizens.

California’s election personnel have raised concern that the administration’s directive could disenfranchise citizens. Los Angeles officials said this week a “high percentage” of the individuals on the list were born in the United States.

“Trump’s DOJ is so desperate to invent ‘widespread voter fraud,’ it sent California counties lists of people who NEVER voted – and voters from the WRONG COUNTY. Absolute clown show!” California’s governor Gavin Newsom posted on social media.
“Voter intimidation has no place in our democracy,” Pete Aguilar, a congressman representing south-west San Bernardino county, said in a social media post.
The federal government’s oversight attempts come amid a national Republican effort to crack down on alleged voter fraud, particularly any cases among undocumented immigrants.

“We are asking each county election official to commit to working with us by providing the necessary information for DHS to quickly verify citizenship status. With their help, we can ensure the most secure election in California history,” the justice department said.
Rob Bonta, the California attorney general, has raised questions about the evidence behind the suspected noncitizen ballots.

“All they provided was a list of people and nothing about why they’re purportedly ineligible. If they have such information, we would be happy to review it, but they’ve provided none,” Bonta said at a recent press conference.
The DoJ also charged 28 foreign nationals recently, accusing them of fraudulently registering to vote.

“Today’s arrests prove what we have been saying,” Bill Essayli, first assistant US attorney, said in a statement. “California is mailing ballots to noncitizens, and they are refusing to comply with federal law, which makes it a crime for noncitizens to vote. The voting rights of American citizens must be protected.”
Some state officials took no action, citing the fast-approaching election, which spurred a legal battle with the justice department. An appeals court is set to hear the matter on Tuesday.

articles.title: Barack Obama rallies Michigan crowd for El-Sayed, saying he’s ‘fighting for real change’
articles.summary:
Former president speaks to rapturous crowd of thousands in support of Democrat Abdul El-Sayed for US Senate

Barack Obama told a Detroit crowd on Saturday that Abdul El-Sayed was “fighting…

blocks.text: Barack Obama told a Detroit crowd on Saturday that Abdul El-Sayed was “fighting for change, real change, that will get money out of politics and put money in your pocket”, as he threw his weight behind the Democratic Senate candidate and the rest of the ticket on the first day of early voting in Michigan.

Obama said in front of thousands of onlookers at Cass technical high school in Detroit that El-Sayed would “finish the job we started with the Affordable Care Act and guarantee quality, affordable healthcare to every single American”.

The former president headlined the rally for El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for US Senate, and secretary of state Jocelyn Benson, the party’s candidate for governor, at an evening event to “get out the vote”.

He accused Donald Trump of “enriching himself and his family”, and said the administration had set a “culture … at the top” of taking favors. “Never seen a president so intent on selling favors like this,” he said.

The rally came on the first day of Michigan’s early voting period, with the general election on 3 November. It was also Obama’s first weekend of in-person campaigning during the midterms, which started in Cleveland, Ohio, earlier in the day to stump for the former Ohio senator Sherrod Brown and Democratic nominee for governor Amy Acton earlier in the weekend. He issued similarly scathing remarks aimed at the White House and the GOP.

blocks.caption: Abdul El-Sayed speaks to supporters during a campaign rally in Detroit on Saturday. Photograph: Paul Sancya/AP

blocks.text: The Detroit stop is Obama’s first public show of support for El-Sayed, who emerged from a bitter August primary in which the former president stayed on the sidelines. El-Sayed, a doctor and former Wayne county health official, beat the moderate congresswoman Haley Stevens who was riding on the backing of the Democratic establishment and pro-Israel organizations.

Obama was on the offensive against the administration, mocking the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, as “laser-focused” on the “jawline and testosterone levels of our troops”, asking: “How much time do you think this man spends in front of the mirror every day?”

On tariffs, Obama said Trump was toughest on “that well-known evil empire”, referring to Canada, a few minutes’ drive from Detroit across the bridge. “These are the people who gave us Martin Short and maple syrup,” he said.

Questions had hung over whether Obama would back El-Sayed at all. El-Sayed, a champion of Medicare for All, had at one point called the Affordable Care Act, Obama’s signature domestic achievement, an incremental fix. The two men spoke by phone after the primary, and El-Sayed has since called Obama a mentor figure.

blocks.caption: The rally for Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit on Saturday. Photograph: Paul Sancya/AP

blocks.text: El-Sayed has the most ground to make up in Wayne county, where Detroit is the county seat, after Stevens beat him there by about 51% to 45% in the August primaries. Obama last campaigned in Detroit – which is more than three-quarters Black – in October 2024 for Kamala Harris, and Harris herself appeared with El-Sayed in Detroit last month.

Republicans have not held a Michigan Senate seat in 25 years, but the party sees the seat as one of its better pickup chances nationwide. El-Sayed faces Mike Rogers, a former congressman endorsed by Donald Trump who lost a 2024 Senate matchup against Democratic senator Elissa Slotkin by less than half a percentage point. The Cook Political Report rates this race a toss-up.

Slotkin, a featured speaker at the rally, told the crowd that “Michigan believes in electing fighters”. And when it came to any disagreements she may have with El-Sayed, she said: “It’s OK because we agree on so much more.”
“We’re putting a check and balance on Donald Trump in the White House,” she said.

A Marist poll of likely voters statewide conducted in mid-October put El-Sayed at 50% and Rogers at 48%, within the margin of error. RealClearPolitics’s average had El-Sayed ahead by about 2.6 points in a similar timeframe.

blocks.caption: Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters during the campaign rally in Detroit on Saturday. Photograph: Paul Sancya/AP

blocks.text: Trump has attacked El-Sayed throughout the campaign, calling him a “jihadist”, pointing to his middle name and alleging that he had ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, which El-Sayed strongly denies, and has created one of the most viral moments of the year. El-Sayed has also faced a barrage of criticism from the establishment wing of the Democratic party over his appearances with leftwing streamer Hasan Piker.

Trump is due in the state himself on Sunday, when he will hold a rally for Michigan Republicans in Port Huron, on the Canadian border. The city said it will be the first presidential visit to St Clair county.

If elected, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim and first Egyptian American in the US Senate. Benson faces the Republican congressman John James; a James win would make him Michigan’s first Black governor.

Turning to the disagreements between them, Obama acknowledged that some people had pointed out that El-Sayed “didn’t like some things you did as president”. “We are not going to agree on every detail of every issue,” he said. “You know who else doesn’t agree with everything I do? Michelle Obama.”
“We share those values of making sure everybody gets a fair shot in this society,” Obama said, “and that the system’s not just run for those at the top.”

articles.title: Voters in Brazil to choose between Lula and Bolsonaro's son
articles.summary: Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of Brazil's imprisoned former president, is presenting a strong challenge to Lula, 80, who is seeking a fourth term in office.

blocks.text: Never before has a candidate who trailed after the first round managed to overturn the deficit and win in the second round.

Bolsonaro's supporters were jubilant at his final campaign rallies, confident that he would bring change to Brazil through his promised tough crackdown on organised crime, as well as tax and public spending cuts.
He campaigned on the eve of polls in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais, which has been a must-win state for any presidential hopeful since the 1980s.
"The time is almost here," Bolsonaro told supporters in a social media video.
"There are only a few hours left before we shape the future of our nation for the next 30 or 40 years."
He has also pledged to release his father, who is currently serving his sentence under house arrest due to ill health.
In Barra de Tijuca, Rio de Janeiro, where Jair Bolsonaro has a home, Bolsonaro supporters rallied in support of him dressed in the national colours.
"Brazil needs change, and Flávio is the person that represents that today, after so many years of the Left destroying the economy and the country," one told BBC News.
Another said that what she most liked about Flávio Bolsonaro was his promise to "end violence in Brazil, end terrorism, narco-trafficking, and to reduce interest rates".

articles.title: Nigeria: Tinubu launches reelection bid amid economic woes
articles.summary: President Bola Tinubu promised "a better tomorrow" for Nigerians while kicking off his next electoral campaign, while also blaming his rivals for poverty plaguing Africa's most populous nation.

image.caption: Tinubu said his administration is confronting Nigeria's economic crisisImage: Marvellous Durowaiye/REUTERS

blocks.text: Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu on Saturday formally launched his campaign for a second term.
"We have prosperity, consistency, growth, recovery and opportunity," Tinubu said at a rally in the northwestern state of Kaduna.
"You grant me the privilege to promise you once again, there is that promise of a better tomorrow," he added.
Africa's most populous country will hold its next presidential election in January 2027. The campaign is expected to focus on Nigeria's economy and security challenges.
Tinubu's tax gamble: Progress or pain for Nigerians?
Nigeria's worsening cost of living
After taking power in 2023, Tinubu sparked anger by scrapping decades-long fuel subsidies — a move that has fueled Nigeria's inflation.
On Saturday, the incumbent president dismissed criticisms about his economic policies.
"I hear my opponents talking about hunger and poverty. Who created it? They did," Tinubu said at the crowded rally. "They created the hunger, they created the poverty. We are trying to eradicate it."

Earlier this month, the 74-year-old acknowledged Nigeria's economic issues. In his Independence Day address, he argued that his administration's reform "did not create the weaknesses in our economy," but actually "confronted them."
Tinubu's government announced potential price caps on fuel soon after.
Security threats to play big role in Nigeria's election
Apart from grappling with a cost-of-living crisis, Nigeria continues to struggle with armed bandits and kidnappers.
On Friday, gunmen killed at least 20 people in an attack on a village in the country's northeast.
The nation has also been fighting a long-running jihadist insurgency, sparked by Boko Haram's 2009 uprising.

blocks.caption: Thousands of supporters showed up in Kaduna for Tinubu's first election campaign of the seasonImage: Sani Maikatanga/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Another three-man race
Tinubu's main challengers are expected to be former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and former state governor Peter Obi.
In the 2023 presidential election,Tinubu only managed to secure less than 36.6% of the valid votes cast, with Abubakar at 29% and Obi at 25.4%.
Is Nigeria becoming a one-party state?

articles.title: Polls close in less than an hour as British Columbians choose next provincial government

image.caption: The Greens' watch party in Central Saanich tonight. (Emily Fagan/CBC)

items: October 25Green supporters optimistic ahead of polls closingThe Greens' watch party in Central Saanich tonight. (Emily Fagan/CBC)I'm at Church and State Winery in Central Saanich where about 100 B.C. Green Party supporters are gathered. There's a bubbling excitement in the room as people enter, grabbing snacks from a charcuterie board and posing in a photo booth.

Gunn, Merrifield in attendance at B.C. Conservative watch partyTarnjit ParmarSupporters at the B.C. Conservative election night watch party tonight. (Tarnjit Parmar/CBC)I’m a producer with CBC News at the B.C. Conservative Party election night watch party at Rocky Mountaineer Station in Vancouver. Doors have opened and supporters are pouring into the venue. Aaron Gunn, the federal Conservative MP for North Island-Powell River is in attendance as is Katy Merrifield, campaign director for the B.C. Conservatives. Merrifield faced criticism over anti-Islam posts shared on social media earlier this year. Sam Sullivan, the former mayor of Vancouver and two-time MLA under the B.C. Liberals, has also made an appearance. A number of former staffers from the B.C. Liberals tell us they are happy to be here tonight to offer their support to B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson. We are being told that around 1,300 people will be here tonight, as results roll in from around the province after polls close at 8 p.m. PT.

NDP headquarters are quiet as the clock ticks downNadia JannifThe NDP headquarters in Vancouver. (Nadia Jannif/CBC)I'm working alongside provincial affairs reporter Katie DeRosa tonight at B.C. NDP headquarters in downtown Vancouver. The room is lit up and ready, but mostly empty as various media outlets prepare for election results to come in. Polls close in less than 10 minutes.

U.S. trade dispute, bid for stronger majority among Eby's reasons for election callRhianna SchmunkEby calls snap B.C. election citing 'existential' Trump threatB.C. NDP Leader David Eby called an early provincial election to be held on Oct. 24, citing the 'existential' threat of U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war on Canada. Eby also dismissed questions about the ethics of calling the vote while the B.C. Conservative Party is in disarray.When Eby called the early provincial election, he presented the vote as British Columbians' chance to choose which government will meet the "existential" threat posed by the trade dispute between Canada and the United States. But he distanced himself from that rationale as the campaign progressed, making no mention of the Trump administration or the U.S. president's name in response to a question about his snap election decision during the leaders' debate on Oct. 14.Eby has also said his party needs a stronger majority, with its current one-seat margin preventing his government from doing "what needs to be done" because it was too fragile — citing the need for every party MLA to vote every time to ensure its legislation is passed. He said another election couldn't wait even a few weeks until after last week's local elections because he believed the political landscape has changed so dramatically since his government was elected two years ago.Candidates from opposing political parties criticized the early election as "cynical," though they have welcomed an opportunity for change in Victoria after nine years of NDP rule.

The B.C. NDP's platformAkshay KulkarniDavid Eby makes the case for another 4 yearsDavid Eby is asking British Columbians for another four years as premier. But after calling a snap election with the opposition party in chaos, the NDP is now facing a serious challenge from the B.C. Conservatives. The CBC's Katie DeRosa looks at Eby's promises, setbacks, and the political gamble that will determine his future.The NDP's platform is largely built on continuing the work it's done over its past nine years in power — particularly by boosting health-care recruitment from the U.S and reducing the province's reliance on its southern neighbour through major projects. The party's platform predicts the province's deficit will fall by $2 billion over two years, according to its costing, some of which is predicated on income tax increases for the top 3.88 per cent of earners in B.C.The NDP is also promising to freeze auto insurance rates for three years; a temporary 10 per cent reduction of the provincial fuel tax; and an expansion of vacancy and speculation taxes to increase housing development.

Unknown factor could be an asset for Doerkson and the ConservativesKatie DeRosaDoerkson during a campaign stop in Sidney, B.C., on Tuesday. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)Doerkson is the first person to admit he did not set out to become the leader of the B.C. Conservative Party. "Of course, it was a little bit of a short notice," Doerkson told CBC News earlier this month from his home in Williams Lake, B.C., in his signature understated tone.While people across the political spectrum describe Doerkson, 58, as a nice guy, he's an unelected and largely unknown party leader who has been finding his feet in the election campaign. Andrew Reeve, a former B.C. Liberal communications director who worked alongside Doerkson in that caucus, said that could be a source of strength for the two-term MLA."There's that old adage of perhaps we should give power to those who don't seek it, and I think that really fits the type of guy that Lorne is," Reeve told me earlier this month. "The person that'll lend you their truck or they'll give you a ride home from the airport."

The B.C. Conservatives' platformAkshay KulkarniUnexpected leader: Lorne Doerkson pitches himself to British ColumbiansB.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson finds himself in an unprecedented situation. Doerkson is set to make his main pitch to British Columbians on the debate stage Wednesday night. Katie DeRosa caught up with Doerkson at his home in Williams Lake.While the Conservatives were in disarray little more than a month ago — facing a number of splinter parties and an unpopular leader — when the snap election was called they quickly coalesced around Doerkson, who initially assumed his role on an interim basis. The party's platform has focused on attacking the NDP's near-decade in office and promising to rein in the province's deficit. According to the Conservatives' platform, if they are elected the province's deficit would fall to $10.8 billion by 2030, with the party promising to freeze outside hiring, cut consultants and review spending across ministries to find billions in savings.The party has promised to complete the new Surrey Hospital and B.C. Cancer Centre, and build a new women's and children's hospital in Surrey. It has pledged to expand detox and treatment services, along with ending the safe supply of drugs, to deal with the toxic drug crisis.In addition, the Conservatives have promised to replace the George Massey Tunnel in Delta with a 10-lane bridge, largely scrap the province's no-fault auto insurance model and repeal the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act.

Green leader aims to hold the balance of powerEmily FaganLowan during the B.C. election provincial leaders’ debate in Vancouver on Oct. 14. (Ethan Cairns/CBC)Last year, in a campaign that echoed the style of Zohran Mamdani's push to become New York mayor, Lowan became one of the youngest people elected to lead a political party in Canada.Without a seat in the legislature — of which the Greens held two — she's spent much of the past year touring the province to build grassroots support.Lowan, 26, hopes to win the balance of power in Victoria — but first, needs to win herself a seat. She's running in Saanich North and the Islands, a riding formerly held by the Greens' Rob Botterell."I think my ask to voters is, I'm not going to be premier in a week, but I do want the B.C. Greens to hold a minority government to account," she told CBC News.The Greens will have "terms and conditions" for any party they work with, she says, and did not rule out striking a deal with the B.C. Conservatives to form government."Nothing's off the table," she said.Lowan says over its nine years in power, the NDP has broken trust with First Nations, abandoned climate promises and let affordability challenges spiral.

The B.C. Greens' platformAkshay KulkarniLowan in North Saanich, B.C., on Thursday. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)The B.C. Green Party entered the snap election campaign with their leader not having a seat in the legislature — and Lowan has argued that voters should send Green MLAs to Victoria to keep the other two major parties in check, ideally through a minority government.Lowan's party is critical of both the NDP's record in office and the Conservatives' positions on key issues.Its platform has pledged a windfall tax on mega-corporations and making B.C.'s richest people pay more — with a proposed "Fair Share Act" predicted to raise $22.2 billion in its first year and $5.4 billion every year thereafter — and promises to expand union jobs in areas like renewable energy.The Greens have promised to lift the NDP's freeze on new $10-a-day child-care spaces, and pledged that every British Columbian would have free and universal child care by 2031. The party's platform includes promises of free transit; an expansion of community health centres; expanding non-market housing along with vacancy control; and boosting harm-reduction measures to deal with the toxic drug crisis.

CentreBC's platformAkshay KulkarniCentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko has said her fledgling party aims to give a voice to those feeling politically homeless. (Hunter Soo/CBC)CentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko was one of many former B.C. Conservative MLAs that joined the fledgling party amid chaos in the Tories' caucus. But she ended up being the lone high-profile MLA left standing after many CentreBC members rejoined the Conservatives under Doerkson.Sturko has told CBC News that her party wants to provide a home for centrist voters who feel alienated by both the Conservatives and the NDP, saying CentreBC has fiscally responsible, socially progressive policies.The party has pledged to push for hiring hundreds more provincial RCMP officers if its candidates are elected, along with increasing the renter's tax credit and providing more seats in schools.

articles.title: Four people injured after drive-by shooting outside boxing event south of Brisbane
articles.summary:
Offenders still at large after shots fired from vehicle outside licensed premises in Loganholme

  • Get our breaking…

blocks.text: Four people have been injured after a drive-by shooting outside a venue hosting a boxing event.
Police said they responded to reports of shots being fired from a vehicle outside a licensed premises in Loganholme, south of Brisbane, at 8.15pm.
“The involved vehicle was witnessed leaving the scene,” police said.
Fitzys Loganholme on Bryants Road was scheduled to host the Logan City Titles Fight Night on Saturday.
Four injured people were taken to hospital, police said, and their condition was being assessed.
The offenders are still at large but police said they did not believe there was an ongoing threat to the public.
Police were urging anyone with information about the incident to contact them.
More details soon …

articles.title: Andy Burnham says he wants ‘honest discussion’ about freedom of movement with EU
articles.summary:
Prime minister is considering different options for new relationship with Brussels ahead of summit in November

Andy Burnham says he wants an “honest discussion” with the British public about…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham says he wants an “honest discussion” with the British public about the possibility of a return to free movement between the UK and the EU as part of his plans for a new relationship with the bloc.
The prime minister has been open about his desire to revisit the relationship between Britain and Brussels. He has said a new deal could mean the UK goes “all the way” and rejoins the EU.

Other options discussed by Burnham include joining the single market, which would require signing up to free movement, or being part of the customs union. Both would require an element of agreeing to rules set by the EU.
In an interview with the Sunday Times he said: “I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this.”
The prime minister has previously committed to the red lines in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
It means any fundamental change in the relationship is likely to have to wait until after a general election, expected by 2029.
The prime minister acknowledged freedom of movement “had very significant challenges associated with it”, but suggested that European migration had changed in the past decade.
“It was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now],” he told the Sunday Times.
“Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different.
“The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”
Burnham will meet EU chiefs at a summit in Brussels on 20 November.
He argued that there had been reciprocal benefits of free movement for Britons, particularly for young members of the population wanting to experience living in Europe.
The issue of migration was one of the dominant debates during the 2016 Brexit referendum campaign.
In the 12 months to June 2016 – the month of the Brexit leave vote – net migration was at a near-record high of 335,000, according to the Office for National Statistics.
Decisions made after the Brexit result would lead to higher levels of migration, however.

Net migration peaked at a record 944,000 in the year to March 2023 due to a surge of foreign workers encouraged to come to the UK by Boris Johnson’s Conservative government as the UK emerged from the Covid pandemic.
It has fallen sharply since then, with net migration dropping to well below pre-Brexit levels. It stood at 171,000 last year, almost half of what it was in 2016.
Burnham has said he will take the opportunity around the summit with EU leaders in November to lay out to the British public different options for the future relationship with the bloc.
But Burnham added that he could not imagine recommending that the UK join the Schengen Area, in which border controls have been abolished, or ditching the pound to adopt the euro.
Nigel Farage said the prime minister’s comments were a “total betrayal” of voters who backed Brexit, including in Burnham’s Makerfield constituency.
The Reform UK leader added: “He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty.”

Chris Philp, the Conservative shadow home secretary, said: “Andy Burnham knows full well that a return to EU free movement would mean handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe.
“The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it.”

articles.title: The bitter row over military service that could shape Israel's future
articles.summary: The ultra-Orthodox community is resisting being drafted into the Israeli army. But will they now bring down the Netanyahu government?

blocks.text: BySebastian Usher

blocks.caption: Sebastian Usher

blocks.text: Furious protesters are denouncing Israeli security forces as "Nazis" - but this is not a scene from a pro-Palestinian rally on the streets of London or Paris. This clash is in the heart of Israel, in which hundreds of ultra-Orthodox men in white shirts, black fedoras and long black frock coats face off against the military police.

The flashpoint is a building in the city of Modi'in, midway between Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, where a young ultra-Orthodox Jewish (or Haredi) man lives. The police have come to arrest him after he failed to report for military service.
The clash in early October, seen by the BBC in a video, is one of many in recent months in which one of the deepest schisms in Israeli society has become ever more exposed.

This widening fault line is playing out against the backdrop of the wars Israel is currently fighting, including the unresolved conflict against Hamas in Gaza - as well as increasing violence by extremist settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

Once a tiny minority, the ultra-Orthodox remain a group apart even as their numbers expand year by year. Currently, they are estimated to make up about 14% of the population, and the birth rate within the community remains far higher than among other Israelis. If their numbers continue to grow at a similar rate, they could make up one-third of the Jewish Israeli population by 2050.

As the ultra-Orthodox community becomes bigger, so has the debate around the expense of supporting them with stipends so they can devote themselves to full-time religious study. Subsidies to the group are estimated to cost the government 35bn shekels (£8.4bn) per year and, until recently, they were exempted from military service.
Now they're no longer an insignificant minority, they're facing pressure to engage more with wider Israeli society.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ultra-Orthodox Jews have staged many protests against being drafted into the military

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Ultra-Orthodox Jews have staged many protests against being drafted into the military

National security and the economy are two of the key issues this election. That means the division between the ultra-Orthodox and the majority of Israelis who believe they are not contributing their fair share to either is starker than ever.

With no outright majority likely for any current political alliance, and the future of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in doubt, the role of smaller parties - including Haredi parties - will once again be crucial in deciding who will govern Israel.
To have any chance of staying in power, Netanyahu needs to keep the ultra-Orthodox parties on side, however much pressure there is within Israel for their special status to be diminished.
A group apart

From the ultra-Orthodox perspective, their social contract with the Israeli state is increasingly coming under pressure. Their all but exclusive focus on the study of Judaism's religious texts - such as the Torah, the Jewish Bible - means their education system is separate and many Haredim are not part of Israel's workforce.

For the ultra-Orthodox, the biggest issue of all is holding on to the exemption from serving in the IDF for students at traditional religious - or yeshiva - institutions. This dates back to the earliest days of the Israeli state when the Haredim were a miniscule community of survivors struggling to rebuild from the near extinction of the Holocaust.

But as Israel has become more embattled after the attacks of October 7, fighting wars on several fronts, their near complete absence from the country's conscription army has become more controversial.

Religious students and their rabbis believe that if young ultra-Orthodox men enter the military, they will be exposed to influences and behaviours that may decisively turn them away from their community. Beyond that, they believe that their staying true to the traditions of their community is vital for the very survival not only of Israel but the Jewish people.

When asked not long after October 7 why the ultra-Orthodox didn't contribute more to the military in such an emergency, one of the community's most senior leaders, Rabbi Dov Landau, said that not only should religious students not serve in the army, but they shouldn't even visit the wounded or attend the funerals of soldiers.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The Haredi birth rate is higher than in the rest of Israeli society

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
The Haredi birth rate is higher than in the rest of Israeli society

The rabbi said that in a time of such danger, only Torah students could protect Israel spiritually. "Salvation only comes through Torah learning, orderly Torah learning. And any neglect of or disruption to Torah learning, woe and alas for what will happen… The more Torah learners multiply, the more Torah learners increase their learning, the better. They protect us."

It would be a considerable understatement to say that this view is not shared by wider Israeli society. Polls have shown public support for conscripting the ultra-Orthodox surge throughout the war in Gaza. Many see it as a dereliction of responsibility by the Haredi community, made all the more galling by the fact that such a stance comes at the expense of taxpayers. The IDF has bemoaned a deficit in manpower, while many Israelis have had to serve hundreds of days in the past three years.

Dahlia Scheindlin is a leading political consultant and pollster in Israel. She says this issue is critical for Netanyahu and is key to understanding this moment in Israeli society against the backdrop of the war in Gaza, particularly among the political right. "Really the most burning, more immediate issue is the right-wing communities who are furious at the government for protecting the blanket exemption from the IDF at a time when, especially among the right, but really everybody in the Jewish community in Israel, is serving and many dying in these wars."

Two years ago, the Supreme Court ruled that the exemption for ultra-Orthodox men from serving in the military was effectively null and void. That could have meant that those dedicated to full-time religious study would now be drafted.

The reaction from the Haredi community was one of fury. Hundreds of thousands of Haredim held protests, blocking the main highways. And as with the incident in Modi'in, they tried to prevent the arrest of religious students for evading conscription. Protests have continued off and on, and densely-populated Haredi areas are often the backdrops for confrontation with the security forces.
Consequences at the polls
This is a row that is playing out in the election.

There are two parties that have traditionally represented the Haredi community. One is United Torah Judaism – or UTJ – and represents Ashkenazi Jews, or Jews of European origin. The other is Shas, which was formed later and represents the Sephardi and Mizrahi – Jews from North Africa and the Middle East. They share a core agenda, which puts religious study above all else, including any questions around relations with the Palestinians.

Both UTJ and Shas have been part of Netanyahu's coalition - and they used their political clout to find ways to try to block enforcement of the Supreme Court ruling. On several occasions, they threatened to pull out of the alliance and bring the government down. UTJ acted on this but continued to support the government from outside, while Shas remained within the coalition.

Centre-right politician Gadi Eisenkot, who's shaped up as Netanyahu's main rival in this month's election, does not support their stance. He has made clear his belief that the idea of the ultra-Orthodox constituting a separate state within Israel with its own rules has become increasingly toxic. "A country that sends its best sons and daughters to fight and sacrifice their lives cannot tolerate a reality in which a state within a state exists," he said.
All this has meant that the issue of conscription exemption for ultra-Orthodox men is the number one priority on the electoral agenda of both Shas and UTJ.

A recent remark by a UTJ parliamentary candidate, Eliakim Stark, has raised the temperature further. He compared the plight of ultra-Orthodox men evading the military draft to the persecution of Jews during the Holocaust. It triggered furious rebukes from opposition leaders from across the political spectrum.
Daniel Goldman, an activist who specialises in Haredi issues, says that the two main Haredi parties feel increasingly embattled and less open to compromise.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Protesters have blocked key highways

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Protesters have blocked key highways

He says the ultra-Orthodox don't believe that the state really needs their boys to bolster numbers. "It's at least partly down to the fact that the Haredi parties see the state as wanting to take their boys out of the community and change them from ultra-Orthodox to either regular religious or secular, God forbid, as they perceive it," he says. "And so in that environment of tension, they've actually hardened their positions."

Yitzhak Goldknopf from the UTJ, a former minister, has gone so far as to issue an ultimatum: "The Haredim will not change their way of life because there is an army and a war... If there is no choice and they must leave the country, they will leave."

But this is having a clear impact on the electoral fortunes of the Netanyahu coalition - of which Shas in particular has long been a key part. Without them, Netanyahu's alliance would fall short of the more than 60 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset.

Dahlia Scheindlin, the Israeli pollster, says that the refusal to give up the draft exemption by Shas and UTJ is damaging Netanyahu's coalition. "It is one of the main reasons why the coalition is unable to win back the kind of support that they had in 2022 when they won 64 seats," she says. "They're currently polling at about 50 to 52 seats."

All Netanyahu's challengers advocate for ending the ultra-Orthodox exemption and cutting funds to institutions or individuals who refuse the draft. On the left, Yair Golan has called for an immediate mobilisation of those who are eligible.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Benjamin Netanyahu is relying on Haredi support which may not materialise

blocks.text: Benjamin Netanyahu is relying on Haredi support which may not materialise
So, despite statements from Shas and UTJ that they would switch allegiance from Netanyahu if he were to dilute his support, there seems for now nowhere else for them to go.

Anshel Pfeffer has been a leading commentator on the Israeli political scene for years - now mainly as the Economist's correspondent in Israel. He says Netanyahu's position looks shaky. "There are two things that are bringing together the current opposition bloc," he says. "One is obviously they want to replace Netanyahu and the other is they are capitalising on this really hostile environment nowadays towards the ultra-Orthodox, mainly over the issue of the draft to the army.
"Netanyahu has been willing for many years, to basically give the ultra-Orthodox whatever they want. They're not going to get that from the opposition."
A potential compromise?
Into this arena of resentment and intransigence, a new Haredi party has emerged this year, presenting itself as a break with the traditional mindset of Shas and UTJ.
Essentially, the Haredi Public Party is offering a compromise in which the ultra-Orthodox would contribute more to Israel as a whole while maintaining the core of their identity.
For the first time in the ultra-Orthodox community, it is also fielding two female candidates.

One of them, Ziva Ginz, explained to the BBC her party's position on the military draft. Key to it is men serving being allowed to remain culturally Haredi. "Anyone whose life is genuinely devoted to full-time Torah study should be able to continue learning. Everyone who isn't sitting and studying for a full day should serve alongside the rest of Israeli youth, in frameworks where a young man can enter as a Haredi and finish as a Haredi," she says.
But it may be too soon for such efforts at compromise to make an impact this election.
Anshel Pfeffer says that it's difficult to sway the base vote in the ultra-Orthodox community, where most still essentially follow what their rabbi says they should do.

"And once people are voting for other parties, they won't necessarily do so for another Haredi party," Pfeffer explains. "That's why we're seeing people like [far-right leader and National Security Minister Itamar] Ben-Gvir making inroads in the Haredi community, because he's the only non-Haredi party leader who actually talks to young Haredi. Basically, every other party in Israel doesn't even try."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ben-Gvir is making inroads with Haredi voters

blocks.text: Ben-Gvir is making inroads with Haredi voters
This is reflected in the polls, which show his Jewish Power party is making gains.

If Ben Gvir's actions are increasingly seen as tainting Israel's international image with his support for policies such as annexing the occupied West Bank, his hard-right message is attracting a bigger core of support within the country. His ultra-nationalist ethos is not one that traditionally overlaps with policies of the Haredi parties, but they share a position on the right of Israeli politics.

So for some ultra-Orthodox voters looking for a new political home, Ben Gvir represents the nearest alternative. His self-portrayal as a strong man unafraid to take an extreme position against those he perceives as Israel's enemies in the face of international condemnation may attract some already leaning to the far right in the Haredi community.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Gadi Eisenkot has been firm in his support for Haredi Jews serving in the military

blocks.text: Gadi Eisenkot has been firm in his support for Haredi Jews serving in the military
No alliance appears close to achieving a majority, however, so there is bound to be a lot of horse trading to secure a workable coalition after the vote.
Netanyahu will naturally apply his exceptional political skills to trying to find one way or another to stay in power.

As ever, that leaves the smaller parties with the ability to play the role of kingmaker. That's a role that the ultra-Orthodox parties have been known for in the past. But this time they may not be the decisive factor.

"The truth is, any small party can become a kingmaker," Dahlia Scheindlin says. "I don't think it would take too much to lure the Haredi parties away from Netanyahu... The thing is, though, I don't think the opposition parties will want to lure them in unless they have some promise that they're really prepared to make serious concessions on the draft. The opposition parties are absolutely staking their platforms and their promise to the voters on that issue."
This time, rather than being the kingmakers, it may turn out that the ultra-Orthodox parties help bring down the king.
